title: CPU vs GPU Architecture (CUDA, Tensor Cores, Memory)
description: CPU ve GPU architecture farkları. Parallelization, CUDA programming, tensor cores, memory hierarchy. GPU utilization optimization, training acceleration.

content.level0_basic: CPU: Sequential tasks için optimal, few powerful cores. GPU: Parallel tasks için! Thousands of small cores, matrix ops perfect! AI/ML training GPU'da 10-100× faster. CUDA: NVIDIA GPU programming. Modern GPUs tensor cores var (matrix multiply hardware acceleration). Memory hierarchy: GPU memory fast ama limited. CPU-GPU data transfer bottleneck olabilir!
content.level1_beginner:
**CPU vs GPU Architecture**

**CPU (Central Processing Unit):**

**Design:**
- 4-32 cores (high-end)
- Each core: Very powerful, complex
- High clock speed (3-5 GHz)
- Large cache (MB per core)
- Optimized for: Sequential tasks, branching, complex logic

**Structure:**
```
     CPU
┌──────────────┐
│ Core 1 [====]│ ← Powerful
│ Core 2 [====]│
│ Core 4 [====]│
│ ...          │
│ Core 16 [===]│
└──────────────┘
   Few cores
```

**GPU (Graphics Processing Unit):**

**Design:**
- 1000s-10000s of cores
- Each core: Simple, less powerful
- Lower clock speed (1-2 GHz)
- Smaller cache
- Optimized for: Parallel tasks, data processing

**Structure:**
```
       GPU
┌──────────────┐
│[=][=][=][=]  │ ← Many
│[=][=][=][=]  │   simple
│[=][=][=][=]  │   cores
│... (1000s)   │
└──────────────┘
  Massive parallelism
```

**Why GPU for AI/ML?**

**Matrix multiplication:**

Deep learning = tons of matrix ops!

```python
# Forward pass
Z = W @ X  # Matrix multiply!
```

**CPU approach:**
Sequential, row-by-row.

**GPU approach:**
All elements parallel!

**Example:** 1000×1000 matrix multiply
- CPU: ~1000 operations serially
- GPU: 1000 operations parallel → ~1000× faster!

**Speedup:**
```
Task              | CPU Time | GPU Time | Speedup
------------------|----------|----------|--------
Matrix multiply   | 1.0s     | 0.01s    | 100×
Convolution       | 5.0s     | 0.05s    | 100×
Neural net train  | 10 hours | 30 min   | 20×
```

**GPU Memory Hierarchy:**

**1. Global Memory (VRAM):**
- Size: 8-80 GB
- Speed: Slow (~1 TB/s)
- Accessible by all cores

**2. Shared Memory:**
- Size: KB per block
- Speed: Fast (~10 TB/s)
- Shared within thread block

**3. Registers:**
- Size: Few KB per thread
- Speed: Very fast
- Private to thread

**Hierarchy:**
```
┌──────────────────┐
│   Registers      │ ← Fastest, smallest
├──────────────────┤
│ Shared Memory    │ ← Fast, KB
├──────────────────┤
│ Global Memory    │ ← Slower, GB
│   (VRAM)         │
└──────────────────┘
```

**Key concept:** Minimize global memory access, maximize register/shared memory use!
content.level2_application:
**CUDA Programming Basics:**

CUDA = NVIDIA's GPU programming platform.

**Key Concepts:**

**1. Kernel:**
GPU function, runs on all threads.

```cpp
__global__ void vectorAdd(float* A, float* B, float* C, int N) {
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (i < N) {
        C[i] = A[i] + B[i];  // Each thread: one element
    }
}
```

**2. Thread Hierarchy:**

```
Grid (entire GPU)
  └─ Blocks (groups)
       └─ Threads (workers)
```

**Example:** 1024 elements
- Grid: 4 blocks
- Each block: 256 threads
- Total: 4 × 256 = 1024 threads

**3. Memory Management:**

```cpp
// Allocate GPU memory
cudaMalloc(&d_A, size);

// Copy CPU → GPU
cudaMemcpy(d_A, h_A, size, cudaMemcpyHostToDevice);

// Launch kernel
vectorAdd<<<blocks, threads>>>(d_A, d_B, d_C, N);

// Copy GPU → CPU
cudaMemcpy(h_C, d_C, size, cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost);

// Free GPU memory
cudaFree(d_A);
```

**PyTorch/TensorFlow:**

CUDA details hidden, automatic!

```python
# PyTorch
import torch

# Move to GPU
device = torch.device('cuda')
tensor = torch.randn(1000, 1000).to(device)

# Operations on GPU automatically!
result = tensor @ tensor.T  # Matrix multiply on GPU
```

**Tensor Cores:**

Modern GPUs (V100, A100, H100): Specialized hardware!

**Purpose:** Accelerate matrix multiply (FP16/BF16).

**Performance:**
```
Operation        | CUDA Cores | Tensor Cores | Speedup
-----------------|------------|--------------|--------
FP32 matrix mul  | 15 TFLOPS  | -            | -
FP16 matrix mul  | 30 TFLOPS  | 120 TFLOPS   | 4×
```

**Mixed Precision Training:**

Leverage tensor cores!

```python
# PyTorch
from torch.cuda.amp import autocast, GradScaler

scaler = GradScaler()

for data, target in dataloader:
    with autocast():  # FP16 forward pass
        output = model(data)
        loss = criterion(output, target)
    
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()  # FP32 gradients
    scaler.step(optimizer)
    scaler.update()
```

**Benefits:**
- 2-4× faster training
- 50% less memory
- Same accuracy (with gradient scaling)

**CPU-GPU Data Transfer:**

**Bottleneck:** PCIe bandwidth!

```
CPU ←→ PCIe ←→ GPU
      ~16 GB/s  ← Bottleneck!
```

**Optimization:**

**1. Batch processing:**
Transfer large batches, not single samples.

**2. Pinned memory:**
Faster CPU-GPU transfer.

```python
# PyTorch
dataloader = DataLoader(
    dataset,
    batch_size=256,
    pin_memory=True  # ✓ Faster transfer
)
```

**3. Overlap computation + transfer:**
CUDA streams for async operations.

**4. Keep data on GPU:**
Minimize transfers!

```python
# Bad: Transfer every batch
for batch in dataloader:
    batch = batch.to('cuda')  # ❌ Slow
    ...

# Good: Keep on GPU
data = dataset.to('cuda')  # Once!
for batch in data:
    ...  # ✓ No transfer
```

**GPU Utilization:**

**Monitor:**
```bash
nvidia-smi
```

**Output:**
```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| GPU  Name        Temp  GPU-Util  Memory-Usage |
|=============================================================================|
|   0  RTX 3090     45C    95%     22000MiB / 24000MiB |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

**Goals:**
- GPU-Util: 90-100% (GPU busy!)
- Memory: High (but not OOM)

**Low utilization reasons:**
- Batch size too small
- CPU bottleneck (data loading)
- Too many CPU-GPU transfers
content.level3_advanced:
**Advanced Memory Management:**

**Unified Memory:**

Automatic CPU-GPU memory management.

```cpp
// CUDA
cudaMallocManaged(&data, size);  // Accessible from CPU & GPU!

// Use on CPU
data[0] = 1.0;

// Use on GPU
kernel<<<blocks, threads>>>(data);

// Automatic transfer!
```

**PyTorch:**
```python
# Check memory
torch.cuda.memory_allocated()  # Bytes allocated
torch.cuda.memory_reserved()   # Bytes reserved
torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()  # Peak usage

# Clear cache
torch.cuda.empty_cache()
```

**Gradient Checkpointing:**

Trade compute for memory!

**Problem:** Large models → OOM!

**Solution:** Don't store all activations, recompute in backward pass.

```python
# PyTorch
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint

def forward(x):
    # Without checkpointing: stores activations
    x = layer1(x)
    x = layer2(x)  # Memory!
    x = layer3(x)  # Memory!
    return x

def forward_checkpointed(x):
    # With checkpointing: recompute, save memory
    x = checkpoint(layer1, x)
    x = checkpoint(layer2, x)  # ✓ Less memory
    x = checkpoint(layer3, x)
    return x
```

**Result:**
- Memory: 50-80% reduction
- Training time: 20-30% slower

**Multi-GPU Training:**

**1. Data Parallelism:**

Replicate model on each GPU, split data.

```python
# PyTorch
model = nn.DataParallel(model, device_ids=[0, 1, 2, 3])

# Each GPU:
# - Same model
# - Different batch
# - Gradients averaged
```

**2. Model Parallelism:**

Split model across GPUs.

```python
# Layer 1-5 on GPU 0
self.layers_1_5 = nn.Sequential(...).to('cuda:0')

# Layer 6-10 on GPU 1
self.layers_6_10 = nn.Sequential(...).to('cuda:1')

def forward(x):
    x = self.layers_1_5(x)  # GPU 0
    x = x.to('cuda:1')      # Transfer
    x = self.layers_6_10(x) # GPU 1
    return x
```

**3. Pipeline Parallelism:**

Combine data + model parallelism.

**CUDA Streams:**

Overlap operations!

```python
# PyTorch
stream1 = torch.cuda.Stream()
stream2 = torch.cuda.Stream()

with torch.cuda.stream(stream1):
    output1 = model1(input1)  # Async!

with torch.cuda.stream(stream2):
    output2 = model2(input2)  # Parallel!

# Wait for completion
torch.cuda.synchronize()
```

**Kernel Fusion:**

Combine multiple operations → single kernel.

**Example:**
```python
# Unfused: 3 kernels
y = x + 1      # Kernel 1
z = y * 2      # Kernel 2
w = z ** 2     # Kernel 3

# Fused: 1 kernel
w = ((x + 1) * 2) ** 2  # ✓ Single kernel (JIT fusion)
```

**Benefits:**
- Fewer memory transfers
- Better cache utilization
- Faster!

**PyTorch JIT:**
```python
@torch.jit.script
def fused_operation(x):
    return ((x + 1) * 2) ** 2  # Auto-fused!
```

**NVIDIA GPU Generations:**

| GPU      | Arch    | Tensor Cores | Memory | Use Case        |
|----------|---------|--------------|--------|----------------|
| GTX 1080 | Pascal  | No           | 8 GB   | Old, slow      |
| RTX 2080 | Turing  | Yes (1st)    | 8 GB   | Decent         |
| RTX 3090 | Ampere  | Yes (3rd)    | 24 GB  | Great          |
| A100     | Ampere  | Yes (3rd)    | 40-80GB| Production     |
| H100     | Hopper  | Yes (4th)    | 80 GB  | Cutting-edge   |

**Tensor Core generations:**
- 1st (V100, T4): FP16
- 2nd (RTX 20): FP16 + INT8
- 3rd (A100, RTX 30): FP16 + BF16 + TF32
- 4th (H100): All above + FP8

**Performance Profiling:**

**PyTorch Profiler:**
```python
from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity

with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA]) as prof:
    model(input)

print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="cuda_time_total"))
```

**Output:**
```
---------------------------------  ------------  ------------
Name                               CPU time      CUDA time
---------------------------------  ------------  ------------
aten::matmul                       1.23ms        45.67ms
aten::conv2d                       0.89ms        32.10ms
...
```

**Identify bottlenecks!**
content.level4_expert:
**Hardware-Level Optimization:**

**Warp Execution:**

GPU executes threads in groups (warps) of 32.

**Key:** All 32 threads execute same instruction (SIMT).

**Branch divergence:**
```cpp
if (threadIdx.x < 16) {
    // Half warp does this
} else {
    // Half warp does this
}
// ❌ Divergence! Serialized execution.
```

**Optimization:** Avoid divergence within warps.

**Memory Coalescing:**

Threads in warp access consecutive memory → coalesced (fast).

**Coalesced (GOOD):**
```cpp
int i = threadIdx.x;
A[i] = B[i];  // ✓ Thread 0 → A[0], Thread 1 → A[1], ...
```

**Uncoalesced (BAD):**
```cpp
int i = threadIdx.x;
A[i * stride] = B[i];  // ❌ Non-consecutive access
```

**Bank Conflicts:**

Shared memory divided into banks.

**Conflict:** Multiple threads access same bank → serialized.

**Optimization:** Design access patterns to avoid conflicts.

**Custom CUDA Kernels:**

PyTorch C++ extensions:

```cpp
// kernel.cu
__global__ void my_kernel(float* out, float* in, int N) {
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (i < N) {
        // Custom operation
        out[i] = in[i] * 2.0f + 1.0f;
    }
}
```

```python
# Python
import torch
from torch.utils.cpp_extension import load

# JIT compile
custom_op = load(name="custom_op", sources=["kernel.cu"])

# Use
output = custom_op.forward(input)
```

**When to write custom kernels:**
- Unique operation not in library
- Performance critical bottleneck
- Memory access pattern optimization

**Tensor Core Programming:**

**WMMA (Warp Matrix Multiply-Accumulate):**

```cpp
#include <mma.h>
using namespace nvcuda::wmma;

__global__ void wmma_kernel(...) {
    // Fragments (register tiles)
    fragment<matrix_a, 16, 16, 16, half, row_major> a_frag;
    fragment<matrix_b, 16, 16, 16, half, col_major> b_frag;
    fragment<accumulator, 16, 16, 16, float> c_frag;
    
    // Load
    load_matrix_sync(a_frag, A, 16);
    load_matrix_sync(b_frag, B, 16);
    
    // Compute (on tensor core!)
    mma_sync(c_frag, a_frag, b_frag, c_frag);
    
    // Store
    store_matrix_sync(C, c_frag, 16, mem_row_major);
}
```

**Result:** 10× faster matrix multiply!

**NVLink vs PCIe:**

**PCIe:** CPU ↔ GPU
- Bandwidth: 16-32 GB/s
- Latency: High

**NVLink:** GPU ↔ GPU
- Bandwidth: 300-600 GB/s
- Latency: Low

**Multi-GPU with NVLink:**
```python
# DGX system: NVLink between GPUs
model = nn.DataParallel(model)  # ✓ Fast GPU-GPU comm
```

**GPU Direct Storage:**

Direct disk → GPU (bypass CPU!).

**Traditional:**
```
Disk → CPU RAM → GPU RAM
```

**GPU Direct:**
```
Disk → GPU RAM  ✓ Faster!
```

**Production Optimization Checklist:**

1. ✓ Mixed precision (FP16/BF16)
2. ✓ Batch size: maximize GPU memory
3. ✓ Pin memory (dataloader)
4. ✓ Gradient accumulation (simulate large batch)
5. ✓ Gradient checkpointing (large models)
6. ✓ JIT compile (@torch.jit.script)
7. ✓ Profile: identify bottlenecks
8. ✓ Multi-GPU: data parallelism
9. ✓ Kernel fusion: combine ops
10. ✓ Avoid CPU-GPU transfers in loop

**Cost-Performance Trade-offs:**

| GPU     | Price  | Memory | Training Speed | $/TFLOP |
|---------|--------|--------|----------------|--------|
| RTX 3060| $400   | 12 GB  | 1×             | $40    |
| RTX 3090| $1500  | 24 GB  | 2×             | $37    |
| A100    | $10000 | 80 GB  | 4×             | $25    |
| H100    | $30000 | 80 GB  | 6×             | $20    |

**Recommendation:**
- Research: RTX 3090 / 4090
- Production: A100 (cloud)
- Cutting-edge: H100

codeExamples.title: CPU vs GPU Speed Comparison
codeExamples.code:
import torch
import numpy as np
import time
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

print("="*60)
print("CPU vs GPU PERFORMANCE")
print("="*60)

# Check CUDA availability
if torch.cuda.is_available():
    device_name = torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)
    print(f"\n✓ GPU available: {device_name}")
    print(f"  CUDA version: {torch.version.cuda}")
    print(f"  Memory: {torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0).total_memory / 1e9:.1f} GB")
else:
    print("\n⚠️  No GPU available, using CPU only")
    print("  (Install CUDA for GPU support)")

print("\n" + "="*60)
print("MATRIX MULTIPLICATION BENCHMARK")
print("="*60)

print("""
Deep learning = lots of matrix operations!
Let's compare CPU vs GPU speed...
""")

sizes = [100, 500, 1000, 2000, 3000]
cpu_times = []
gpu_times = []
speedups = []

print("\nSize  | CPU Time | GPU Time | Speedup")
print("-" * 50)

for size in sizes:
    # Create random matrices
    A_cpu = torch.randn(size, size)
    B_cpu = torch.randn(size, size)
    
    # CPU benchmark
    start = time.time()
    C_cpu = torch.matmul(A_cpu, B_cpu)
    cpu_time = time.time() - start
    cpu_times.append(cpu_time)
    
    # GPU benchmark (if available)
    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        A_gpu = A_cpu.to('cuda')
        B_gpu = B_cpu.to('cuda')
        
        # Warmup
        _ = torch.matmul(A_gpu, B_gpu)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        
        # Benchmark
        start = time.time()
        C_gpu = torch.matmul(A_gpu, B_gpu)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()  # Wait for GPU to finish
        gpu_time = time.time() - start
        gpu_times.append(gpu_time)
        
        speedup = cpu_time / gpu_time
        speedups.append(speedup)
        
        print(f"{size:4d}  | {cpu_time:8.4f}s | {gpu_time:8.4f}s | {speedup:6.1f}x")
    else:
        gpu_times.append(0)
        speedups.append(0)
        print(f"{size:4d}  | {cpu_time:8.4f}s | -        | -")

if torch.cuda.is_available():
    print(f"\n💡 GPU is {speedups[-1]:.1f}× faster for large matrices!")
else:
    print("\n💡 Get a GPU for major speedups!")

print("\n" + "="*60)
print("MEMORY USAGE")
print("="*60)

if torch.cuda.is_available():
    # Create large tensor on GPU
    size = 5000
    tensor = torch.randn(size, size).to('cuda')
    
    allocated = torch.cuda.memory_allocated() / 1e9
    reserved = torch.cuda.memory_reserved() / 1e9
    
    print(f"\nTensor size: {size}×{size}")
    print(f"Memory allocated: {allocated:.2f} GB")
    print(f"Memory reserved: {reserved:.2f} GB")
    
    print("\n💡 Monitor GPU memory:")
    print("  torch.cuda.memory_allocated()  # Current usage")
    print("  torch.cuda.memory_reserved()   # Total reserved")
    print("  torch.cuda.empty_cache()       # Clear cache")
    
    # Clean up
    del tensor
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
else:
    print("\nGPU not available for memory demo.")

print("\n" + "="*60)
print("BASIC GPU USAGE PATTERN")
print("="*60)

print("""
PyTorch GPU usage (simple!):

```python
# 1. Define device
device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')

# 2. Move model to GPU
model = MyModel().to(device)

# 3. Move data to GPU
for data, target in dataloader:
    data = data.to(device)
    target = target.to(device)
    
    # 4. Operations on GPU automatically!
    output = model(data)
    loss = criterion(output, target)
    
    # 5. Backward & optimize (on GPU)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
```

✓ That's it! PyTorch handles CUDA details.
""")

# Visualize
if torch.cuda.is_available() and len(speedups) > 0:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))
    
    # Time comparison
    ax = axes[0]
    x = np.arange(len(sizes))
    width = 0.35
    
    ax.bar(x - width/2, cpu_times, width, label='CPU', alpha=0.8)
    ax.bar(x + width/2, gpu_times, width, label='GPU', alpha=0.8)

    ax.legend(fontsize=11)

    # Speedup
    ax = axes[1]

    ax.set_xlabel('Matrix Size', fontsize=12)

codeExamples.title: Mixed Precision Training
codeExamples.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from torch.cuda.amp import autocast, GradScaler
import time
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

print("="*60)
print("MIXED PRECISION TRAINING")
print("="*60)

print("""
Mixed Precision:
  • Forward pass: FP16 (faster, less memory)
  • Gradients: FP32 (numerical stability)
  • Tensor cores: 2-4× speedup!

Requires: Modern GPU (Volta, Turing, Ampere+)
""")

if not torch.cuda.is_available():
    print("\n⚠️  GPU not available. Mixed precision needs CUDA.")
    print("\nExiting demo...")
else:
    device = torch.device('cuda')
    
    # Check GPU capability
    capability = torch.cuda.get_device_capability()
    print(f"\nGPU: {torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}")
    print(f"Compute capability: {capability[0]}.{capability[1]}")
    
    if capability[0] < 7:  # Volta = 7.0
        print("⚠️  This GPU doesn't have tensor cores.")
        print("   (Mixed precision still works but less speedup)")
    else:
        print("✓ Tensor cores available!")
    
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("SIMPLE MODEL")
    print("="*60)
    
    # Define model
    class SimpleModel(nn.Module):
        def __init__(self):
            super().__init__()
            self.fc1 = nn.Linear(1024, 2048)
            self.fc2 = nn.Linear(2048, 2048)
            self.fc3 = nn.Linear(2048, 1024)
            self.fc4 = nn.Linear(1024, 10)
        
        def forward(self, x):
            x = torch.relu(self.fc1(x))
            x = torch.relu(self.fc2(x))
            x = torch.relu(self.fc3(x))
            return self.fc4(x)
    
    model = SimpleModel().to(device)
    
    # Dummy data
    batch_size = 256
    input_size = 1024
    num_batches = 50
    
    print(f"\nModel: 4-layer MLP")
    print(f"Batch size: {batch_size}")
    print(f"Input size: {input_size}")
    print(f"Training batches: {num_batches}")
    
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("FP32 TRAINING (BASELINE)")
    print("="*60)
    
    model_fp32 = SimpleModel().to(device)
    optimizer_fp32 = optim.Adam(model_fp32.parameters(), lr=0.001)
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    
    # Warmup
    for _ in range(5):
        data = torch.randn(batch_size, input_size).to(device)
        target = torch.randint(0, 10, (batch_size,)).to(device)
        output = model_fp32(data)
        loss = criterion(output, target)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer_fp32.step()
        optimizer_fp32.zero_grad()
    
    # Benchmark FP32
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    start = time.time()
    
    for i in range(num_batches):
        data = torch.randn(batch_size, input_size).to(device)
        target = torch.randint(0, 10, (batch_size,)).to(device)
        
        output = model_fp32(data)
        loss = criterion(output, target)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer_fp32.step()
        optimizer_fp32.zero_grad()
    
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    fp32_time = time.time() - start
    fp32_memory = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9
    
    print(f"\nFP32 Training:")
    print(f"  Time: {fp32_time:.2f}s")
    print(f"  Memory: {fp32_memory:.2f} GB")
    
    # Reset memory
    torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
    
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("MIXED PRECISION TRAINING")
    print("="*60)
    
    model_amp = SimpleModel().to(device)
    optimizer_amp = optim.Adam(model_amp.parameters(), lr=0.001)
    scaler = GradScaler()  # Gradient scaling!
    
    print("""
    Key components:
      • autocast(): FP16 forward pass
      • GradScaler: Scale gradients (prevent underflow)
    """)
    
    # Warmup
    for _ in range(5):
        data = torch.randn(batch_size, input_size).to(device)
        target = torch.randint(0, 10, (batch_size,)).to(device)
        
        with autocast():
            output = model_amp(data)
            loss = criterion(output, target)
        
        scaler.scale(loss).backward()
        scaler.step(optimizer_amp)
        scaler.update()
        optimizer_amp.zero_grad()
    
    # Benchmark Mixed Precision
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    start = time.time()
    
    for i in range(num_batches):
        data = torch.randn(batch_size, input_size).to(device)
        target = torch.randint(0, 10, (batch_size,)).to(device)
        
        with autocast():  # FP16 forward
            output = model_amp(data)
            loss = criterion(output, target)
        
        scaler.scale(loss).backward()  # Scaled FP32 backward
        scaler.step(optimizer_amp)
        scaler.update()
        optimizer_amp.zero_grad()
    
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    amp_time = time.time() - start
    amp_memory = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9
    
    print(f"\nMixed Precision Training:")
    print(f"  Time: {amp_time:.2f}s")
    print(f"  Memory: {amp_memory:.2f} GB")
    
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("COMPARISON")
    print("="*60)
    
    speedup = fp32_time / amp_time
    memory_reduction = (1 - amp_memory / fp32_memory) * 100
    
    print(f"\nSpeedup: {speedup:.2f}×")
    print(f"Memory reduction: {memory_reduction:.1f}%")
    
    print("""
    \n💡 Benefits:
      ✓ 2-4× faster (tensor cores!)
      ✓ 30-50% less memory
      ✓ Same accuracy (with gradient scaling)
    
    📝 Best Practice:
      ALWAYS use mixed precision on modern GPUs!
    """)
    
    # Visualize
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))
    
    # Time comparison
    ax = axes[0]
    methods = ['FP32\n(Baseline)', 'Mixed Precision\n(FP16+FP32)']
    times = [fp32_time, amp_time]
    colors = ['lightcoral', 'lightgreen']
    
    bars = ax.bar(methods, times, color=colors, edgecolor='black', linewidth=2)
    ax.set_ylabel('Training Time (seconds)', fontsize=12)
    ax.set_title('Training Speed Comparison', fontsize=14)
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3, axis='y')
    
    # Annotate
    for bar, t in zip(bars, times):
        height = bar.get_height()
        ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width()/2., height,
               f'{t:.2f}s',
               ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=11)
    
    # Speedup annotation
    ax.text(0.5, max(times)*0.9, f'{speedup:.2f}× Speedup!',
           ha='center', fontsize=14, weight='bold',
           bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor='yellow', alpha=0.7))
    
    # Memory comparison
    ax = axes[1]
    memories = [fp32_memory, amp_memory]
    
    bars = ax.bar(methods, memories, color=colors, edgecolor='black', linewidth=2)
    ax.set_ylabel('Peak Memory Usage (GB)', fontsize=12)
    ax.set_title('Memory Usage Comparison', fontsize=14)
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3, axis='y')
    
    # Annotate
    for bar, m in zip(bars, memories):
        height = bar.get_height()
        ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width()/2., height,
               f'{m:.2f}GB',
               ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=11)
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    
    print("\n✓ Mixed precision: Essential for modern deep learning!")

codeExamples.title: GPU Memory Optimization
codeExamples.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint

print("="*60)
print("GPU MEMORY OPTIMIZATION")
print("="*60)

if not torch.cuda.is_available():
    print("\n⚠️  GPU not available.")
    print("\nMemory optimization demo needs CUDA.")
else:
    device = torch.device('cuda')
    
    print(f"\nGPU: {torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}")
    total_memory = torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0).total_memory / 1e9
    print(f"Total memory: {total_memory:.1f} GB")
    
    print("""
    \nMemory bottlenecks in deep learning:
      • Large batch size → OOM!
      • Deep models → activations stored
      • Long sequences (transformers)
    
    Solutions:
      1. Gradient checkpointing
      2. Smaller batch size
      3. Gradient accumulation
      4. Mixed precision
    """)
    
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("GRADIENT CHECKPOINTING")
    print("="*60)
    
    print("""
    Problem: Forward pass stores ALL activations for backward.
    Solution: Don't store, RECOMPUTE in backward!
    
    Trade-off:
      • Memory: 50-80% reduction ✓
      • Time: 20-30% slower ❌
    """)
    
    # Deep model
    class DeepLayer(nn.Module):
        def __init__(self, size):
            super().__init__()
            self.layers = nn.Sequential(
                nn.Linear(size, size),
                nn.ReLU(),
                nn.Linear(size, size),
                nn.ReLU()
            )
        
        def forward(self, x):
            return self.layers(x)
    
    class DeepModel(nn.Module):
        def __init__(self, n_layers, size):
            super().__init__()
            self.layers = nn.ModuleList([DeepLayer(size) for _ in range(n_layers)])
        
        def forward(self, x, use_checkpoint=False):
            for layer in self.layers:
                if use_checkpoint:
                    x = checkpoint(layer, x)  # ✓ Checkpointing
                else:
                    x = layer(x)  # ❌ Store all activations
            return x
    
    n_layers = 50
    size = 1024
    batch_size = 32
    
    print(f"\nModel: {n_layers} deep layers")
    print(f"Hidden size: {size}")
    print(f"Batch size: {batch_size}")
    
    model = DeepModel(n_layers, size).to(device)
    
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("WITHOUT CHECKPOINTING")
    print("="*60)
    
    # Reset memory stats
    torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
    
    x = torch.randn(batch_size, size).to(device)
    
    # Forward
    output = model(x, use_checkpoint=False)
    loss = output.sum()
    
    # Backward
    loss.backward()
    
    memory_no_checkpoint = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9
    print(f"\nPeak memory: {memory_no_checkpoint:.2f} GB")
    
    # Clear
    del output, loss, x
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("WITH CHECKPOINTING")
    print("="*60)
    
    # Reset memory stats
    torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
    
    x = torch.randn(batch_size, size).to(device)
    
    # Forward (with checkpointing)
    output = model(x, use_checkpoint=True)
    loss = output.sum()
    
    # Backward (recomputes!)
    loss.backward()
    
    memory_checkpoint = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9
    print(f"\nPeak memory: {memory_checkpoint:.2f} GB")
    
    memory_saved = (1 - memory_checkpoint / memory_no_checkpoint) * 100
    print(f"\nMemory saved: {memory_saved:.1f}%")
    
    print("""
    \n💡 Gradient checkpointing:
      ✓ Enables training larger models
      ✓ Or larger batch sizes
      ❌ 20-30% slower (recomputation)
    
    Use when: Memory-constrained!
    """)
    
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("GRADIENT ACCUMULATION")
    print("="*60)
    
    print("""
    Problem: Want large batch but OOM!
    Solution: Accumulate gradients over small batches.
    
    Example:
      Want batch=256, but only fit batch=64
      → Accumulate over 4 batches (64×4 = 256)
    """)
    
    print("""
    \n```python
    accumulation_steps = 4
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    
    for i, (data, target) in enumerate(dataloader):
        output = model(data)
        loss = criterion(output, target)
        
        # Scale loss
        loss = loss / accumulation_steps
        loss.backward()  # Accumulate gradients
        
        if (i + 1) % accumulation_steps == 0:
            optimizer.step()  # Update after 4 batches
            optimizer.zero_grad()
    ```
    
    Result: Effective batch = 256, memory = 64!
    """)
    
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("MEMORY MONITORING")
    print("="*60)
    
    print("""
    PyTorch memory functions:
    
    ```python
    # Current allocation
    torch.cuda.memory_allocated()  # Bytes
    
    # Reserved (cached)
    torch.cuda.memory_reserved()
    
    # Peak usage
    torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()
    
    # Reset peak counter
    torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
    
    # Clear cache
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    
    # Memory summary
    print(torch.cuda.memory_summary())
    ```
    """)
    
    # Current stats
    allocated = torch.cuda.memory_allocated() / 1e9
    reserved = torch.cuda.memory_reserved() / 1e9
    
    print(f"\nCurrent GPU memory:")
    print(f"  Allocated: {allocated:.2f} GB")
    print(f"  Reserved: {reserved:.2f} GB")
    print(f"  Free: {total_memory - reserved:.2f} GB")
    
    # Visualize
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(10, 6))
    
    methods = ['Without\nCheckpointing', 'With\nCheckpointing']
    memories = [memory_no_checkpoint, memory_checkpoint]
    colors = ['lightcoral', 'lightgreen']
    
    bars = ax.bar(methods, memories, color=colors, edgecolor='black', linewidth=2)
    ax.set_ylabel('Peak Memory (GB)', fontsize=12)
    ax.set_title(f'Gradient Checkpointing Memory Savings ({n_layers} layers)', fontsize=14)
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3, axis='y')
    
    # Annotate
    for bar, m in zip(bars, memories):
        height = bar.get_height()
        ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width()/2., height,
               f'{m:.2f} GB',
               ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=11)
    
    # Savings annotation
    ax.text(0.5, max(memories)*0.8, f'{memory_saved:.1f}% Memory Saved!',
           ha='center', fontsize=14, weight='bold',
           bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor='yellow', alpha=0.7))
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    
    print("\n✓ Memory optimization: Critical for large models!")
codeExamples.explanation: GPU memory optimization! Gradient checkpointing (trade compute for memory), gradient accumulation (large effective batch), memory monitoring. OOM solutions!

quiz.question: GPU neden AI/ML için CPU'dan faster?
options: Thousands of cores → massive parallelism, matrix ops parallel!
quiz.explanation: GPU thousands of simple cores var! Matrix operations (deep learning core) parallel yapar. CPU few powerful cores, sequential. GPU 10-100× faster AI/ML için!

quiz.question: CUDA nedir?
options: NVIDIA GPU programming platform, kernel yazma, memory management
quiz.explanation: CUDA: NVIDIA GPU programming platform! Custom kernels yaz, GPU parallelism exploit et. PyTorch/TensorFlow CUDA kullanır (automatic, hidden).

quiz.question: Tensor cores ne için?
quiz.explanation: Tensor cores: Specialized hardware modern GPUs'ta! Matrix multiply accelerate eder (FP16/BF16). Mixed precision training ile 2-4× speedup! V100, A100, H100'de var.

quiz.question: Mixed precision training neden?
options: FP16 forward (fast, tensor cores) + FP32 gradients (stability) → 2-4× faster!
quiz.explanation: Mixed precision: FP16 forward pass (fast, tensor cores!) + FP32 gradients (numerical stability). 2-4× speedup, 50% less memory, same accuracy! Always use!

quiz.question: Gradient checkpointing trade-off?
quiz.explanation: Gradient checkpointing: Don't store activations, recompute in backward! 50-80% memory reduction, ama 20-30% slower. Use when memory-constrained (large models)!

quiz.question: CPU-GPU data transfer bottleneck nasıl azaltılır?
options: Large batches, pinned memory, minimize transfers, keep data on GPU!
quiz.explanation: CPU-GPU transfer PCIe bottleneck! Solutions: Large batches (not single samples), pinned memory (pin_memory=True), keep data on GPU, avoid loop transfers!

commonMistakes.mistake: Her iteration data CPU'dan GPU'ya transfer etmek
commonMistakes.why: PCIe bandwidth bottleneck! Thousands of small transfers slow.
commonMistakes.fix: Data GPU'da tut, ya da large batches transfer et.
commonMistakes.example:
# YANLIŞ
for batch in dataloader:
    batch = batch.to('cuda')  # ❌ Her iteration!

# DOĞRU
# Option 1: pin_memory
dataloader = DataLoader(dataset, pin_memory=True)  # ✓

# Option 2: Keep on GPU
data = dataset.to('cuda')  # Once!

# YANLIŞ: FP32 only
output = model(data)  # ❌ Slow

# DOĞRU: Mixed precision
from torch.cuda.amp import autocast, GradScaler
scaler = GradScaler()

with autocast():  # ✓ FP16 forward
    output = model(data)

commonMistakes.mistake: GPU memory full → batch size=1 kullanmak
commonMistakes.fix: Gradient accumulation ya da checkpointing kullan.
commonMistakes.example:
# YANLIŞ
batch_size = 1  # ❌ GPU underutilized

# DOĞRU: Gradient accumulation
batch_size = 32
accumulation_steps = 8  # Effective = 256
# Accumulate gradients  # ✓

commonMistakes.why: GPU async! Time ölçümü yanlış (CPU returns before GPU finishes).
commonMistakes.example:
# YANLIŞ
start = time.time()
output = model(data)  # ❌ Returns immediately!
end = time.time()  # Wrong!

# DOĞRU
start = time.time()
output = model(data)
torch.cuda.synchronize()  # ✓ Wait for GPU
end = time.time()

# Large temporary tensor
temp = torch.randn(10000, 10000).to('cuda')
# Use it...

# Clean up
del temp
torch.cuda.empty_cache()  # ✓

# YANLIŞ: Tek GPU
model.to('cuda')  # ❌ Only GPU 0

# DOĞRU: Multi-GPU
model = nn.DataParallel(model)  # ✓ All GPUs
model.to('cuda')

flashcards.back: CPU: Few powerful cores (4-32), sequential tasks. GPU: Thousands simple cores, massive parallelism! Matrix ops parallel → 10-100× faster AI/ML için!
NVIDIA GPU programming platform. Custom kernels, memory management, parallelism. PyTorch/TensorFlow automatic CUDA kullanır!
Matrix multiply hardware acceleration! FP16/BF16 ops. Modern GPUs (V100, A100, H100). Mixed precision ile 2-4× speedup!
FP16 forward pass (fast, tensor cores!) + FP32 gradients (stability). autocast + GradScaler. 2-4× faster, 50% less memory, same accuracy!
Don't store activations, recompute! 50-80% memory saved, ama 20-30% slower. Use when memory-constrained (large models, batch size).
PCIe bandwidth ~16 GB/s! Solutions: Large batches, pinned memory (pin_memory=True), keep data on GPU, minimize transfers!
Registers (fastest, KB) → Shared memory (fast, KB per block) → Global/VRAM (slower, GB). Minimize global access!
Target 90-100% util! Solutions: Larger batch size, pin_memory, gradient accumulation, mixed precision, avoid CPU-GPU transfers. nvidia-smi monitor!
